papers.title: Autophagy activator AA-20 engages CDK5 to promote lipophagy and improve neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes
papers.summary: This paper describes a new compound called AA-20 that activates autophagy, the cell's waste-clearing process. It specifically boosts a form of autophagy called lipophagy, which clears excess lipids, by interacting with a protein called CDK5. The authors show that this treatment improves symptoms associated with neurodegeneration in their experimental models.
papers.why: Since the abstract gives no neuron-specific or spatial details, its main relevance lies in offering a potential pharmacological tool to modulate autophagy/lipophagy pathways that could later be tested in neuronal or brain tissue contexts relevant to mitophagy research.

papers.title: Neuronal and glial transcriptional states vary with proximity to tangle-bearing neurons in the human entorhinal cortex
papers.summary: This study examines how gene expression in neurons and glial cells in the human entorhinal cortex changes based on their spatial distance from neurons containing tau tangles, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. Using spatial transcriptomics, the researchers likely mapped transcriptional states across tissue sections to reveal gradients of cellular response that depend on proximity to pathology rather than uniform disease effects. This approach helps reveal how local microenvironments around diseased neurons shape surrounding brain tissue at a molecular level.
papers.why: This paper demonstrates how spatial transcriptomics can reveal proximity-dependent cellular states around pathological neurons, directly relevant to applying similar spatial approaches to study mitophagy, autophagy, and interneuron/perineuronal net changes in neurodegenerative contexts.

papers.title: Deubiquitinating Enzymes in Alzheimer's Disease: From Protein Homeostasis to Diverse Pathological Processes.
papers.summary: This paper reviews the role of deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) in Alzheimer's disease, focusing on how they regulate protein homeostasis. DUBs remove ubiquitin tags from proteins, which can affect degradation pathways like the proteasome and autophagy, influencing the buildup of toxic proteins such as amyloid-beta and tau. The review also covers how DUBs contribute to other disease-related processes beyond simple protein clearance, such as inflammation and synaptic dysfunction.
papers.why: Understanding DUB-mediated regulation of protein homeostasis is relevant to mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, which are central to this PhD project's investigation of neurodegenerative mechanisms.
papers.figure: A schematic figure illustrating the ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy pathways and where specific DUBs act to regulate amyloid-beta and tau clearance.

papers.title: Gα  <sub>q</sub>  -mediated contact release is required for efficient mitochondrial quality control
papers.summary: This paper investigates how Gαq signaling controls the release of contact sites between mitochondria and other organelles, a step needed for proper mitochondrial quality control. The authors likely show that disrupting this contact release impairs the cell's ability to identify and remove damaged mitochondria. This mechanism could be relevant to how cells maintain mitochondrial health under stress conditions.
papers.why: Understanding molecular regulators of mitochondrial quality control like contact site release is directly relevant to studying mitophagy mechanisms in neurons, even though this study's abstract doesn't specify a neuronal context.

papers.title: Urolithin A Attenuates Noise-induced Hearing Loss and Is Associated With Increased Cochlear Mitophagy Markers.
papers.summary: This study tests whether Urolithin A, a natural compound known to stimulate mitophagy, can protect the inner ear from noise-induced hearing damage. The researchers found that treated animals had reduced hearing loss after noise exposure, along with higher levels of markers indicating active mitophagy in cochlear tissue. This suggests that boosting mitochondrial quality control may help protect sensory cells from stress-induced damage.
papers.why: This paper reinforces the broader principle that pharmacological enhancement of mitophagy can protect sensory/neural tissue from stress-induced damage, a mechanism directly relevant to studying mitophagy's protective role in neurons and interneurons within the brain.

papers.title: Nanomaterial modulation of lysosomal homeostasis in neurodegenerative proteinopathies: from pathological-protein degradation to re-release and seeding
papers.summary: This paper reviews how engineered nanomaterials can interact with lysosomes and influence the breakdown of toxic proteins involved in neurodegenerative diseases, like amyloid or alpha-synuclein aggregates. It discusses a dual-edged outcome: some nanomaterials help degrade these pathological proteins, while others may disrupt lysosomal function and cause partially degraded fragments to be re-released, potentially seeding further aggregation and spreading pathology. The review likely covers mechanisms, design principles for safer nanomaterials, and implications for therapeutic strategies targeting lysosomal-autophagy pathways.
papers.why: Understanding how nanomaterials affect lysosomal degradation and potential re-release of pathological proteins is directly relevant to mitophagy/autophagy dysfunction in neurons and could inform therapeutic or imaging strategies applicable to interneuron pathology.
papers.figure: A schematic figure illustrating the dual mechanisms of nanomaterial-induced lysosomal protein degradation versus disrupted lysosomal function leading to protein re-release and seeding.

papers.title: Beyond cell replacement: restoring organelle homeostasis as the next frontier of regenerative medicine.
papers.summary: This paper proposes a shift in regenerative medicine away from simply replacing damaged cells and toward restoring the health of cellular organelles like mitochondria and lysosomes. The idea is that many age-related and degenerative diseases stem from organelle dysfunction (e.g., faulty mitophagy or autophagy), and fixing these internal processes could be a more effective therapeutic strategy than cell replacement alone. It positions organelle homeostasis as a new therapeutic target, potentially applicable to neurons and other long-lived cells that cannot easily be replaced.
papers.why: This conceptual framing directly supports the project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy as key regulators of neuronal health, reinforcing the rationale for studying organelle quality control in non-dividing brain cells like interneurons.

papers.title: Chronic Intermittent Hypoxia Aggravates the Pyroptosis of Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells Through Regulating Mitophagy-Mediated NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation.
papers.summary: This study examines how chronic intermittent hypoxia (a hallmark of sleep apnea) affects kidney tubular cells. The researchers found that this hypoxia pattern worsens cell death via pyroptosis by disrupting mitophagy, which leads to activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome. The abstract suggests a mechanistic link between impaired mitochondrial quality control and inflammatory cell death in kidney tissue.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on renal rather than neuronal tissue, it provides mechanistic insight into mitophagy-mediated NLRP3 inflammasome activation, a pathway potentially relevant to neuroinflammation and mitochondrial dysfunction in brain disorders.
